name: Artificial intelligence foundations
summary: What AI is, how it differs from ordinary rules, and how to frame an AI problem.
use: Begin with a defined task and measurable improvement. Adding a model does not automatically make an application more useful.
concepts: Task and objective: Describe the decision or output the system should produce. Define success using observable results rather than vague goals such as making the application intelligent.
Rules versus learned behavior: A rule is explicitly written by a developer. A learned model derives patterns from examples; either approach can be useful depending on the problem.
Uncertainty and evaluation: Model outputs can be wrong even when they look plausible. Evaluate representative cases, important subgroups, and the cost of different mistakes.

name: Machine learning
summary: Training from examples, generalization, datasets, and common learning methods.
use: Generalization means useful behavior on new examples. Memorizing familiar records can produce impressive training results while failing on future cases.
concepts: Features and labels: Features are information available when making a prediction. In supervised learning, labels are the outcomes the model learns to predict.

Training, validation, and test sets: Training examples adjust parameters. Validation supports design choices. A held-out test set estimates performance after those choices, provided it remains genuinely separate.
Learning methods: Supervised learning uses labeled outcomes; unsupervised learning explores structure without those labels. Reinforcement learning optimizes behavior using rewards from interactions.
example: A learner compares three predictions with observed attendance. This demonstrates evaluation, without claiming the supplied predictions came from a trained model.
resumeContext: Study material in my AI learning path. My professional experience is described in the career section.

name: Deep learning and neural networks
summary: Layers, activations, loss, backpropagation, and representation learning.
use: Neural networks can learn useful representations from complex inputs, including language and images. Their flexibility also makes data quality, computing cost, and evaluation especially important.
concepts: Weights and activations: A layer combines inputs using learned weights and biases. A nonlinear activation lets stacked layers represent behavior beyond one linear transformation.
Loss and optimization: A loss measures a chosen kind of prediction error. An optimizer updates parameters using information about how changes would affect that loss.
Backpropagation: Backpropagation efficiently computes gradients through the network using the chain rule. The optimizer then uses those gradients; the two operations are related but distinct.
example: A teaching neuron combines two numbers and applies a rectified linear activation. Its weights are chosen by hand; this is not a trained predictive model.
resumeContext: Study material in my AI learning path. My professional experience is described in the career section.

name: Generative AI
summary: Models that generate text, images, audio, or other data, and where generation is useful.
use: Generation is useful when several acceptable outputs exist, but its variability changes how applications are evaluated. A plausible draft still needs checks appropriate to its intended use.
concepts: Conditioning: Instructions, examples, source material, or other inputs guide the output. These conditions influence generation without becoming a guarantee that every requirement will be satisfied.
Model families: Autoregressive models generate a sequence step by step. Diffusion models learn a denoising process; different families suit different data and tasks.
Generation versus evidence: A generated statement is not its own proof. Source attribution must connect claims to real supporting material rather than invented-looking references.
example: A learner drafts an announcement using three supplied facts: practice is Saturday, the location is Riverside Ground, and arrival is at 08:30.
resumeContext: Study material in my AI learning path. My professional experience is described in the career section.

name: Large language models (LLMs)
summary: Language-model training, next-token prediction, inference, and limits.
use: Learned fluency differs from verified knowledge. Applications need appropriate evidence, boundaries, and task-specific evaluation.
concepts: Pretraining and adaptation: Pretraining learns general patterns from a training objective. Additional supervised or preference-based training can shape behavior, without making every response correct.
Inference: Inference applies a trained model to current input. Ordinary conversation does not automatically update the model's weights or establish permanent memory.
Decoding: A decoder chooses output tokens from model scores according to an inference policy. More variation does not mean more factual accuracy.
example: A club rule permits cancellations until Friday noon. The learner asks whether Friday evening qualifies, using only that rule.
resumeContext: Study material in my AI learning path. My professional experience is described in the career section.

name: Tokens and context windows
summary: Tokenization, context limits, output budgets, and managing conversations.
use: Budget instructions, history, evidence, tool results, and output. A large context does not guarantee correct use of every fact.
concepts: Tokenizer: A tokenizer maps content to token identifiers. Counts vary with the encoding, language, whitespace, and content; words and tokens are not interchangeable units.
Input and output budgets: Input and generation limits interact according to the model's documented rules. Some interfaces also account for internal reasoning or non-text content differently.
Context and memory: Current context is not the same as permanent storage or model training. Applications decide what history or saved facts to supply again.
example: A hypothetical interface has 1,000 units: 600 for input, 250 for output, and 150 for margin. These are teaching values, not a model specification.
resumeContext: Study material in my AI learning path. My professional experience is described in the career section.

name: Transformers and attention
summary: How attention and transformer blocks help models use context.
use: Transformers underlie many language and multimodal models. Their basic mechanics explain contextual representations and several operating costs, without implying that attention weights reveal a complete explanation of a model's decision.
concepts: Queries, keys, and values: Learned projections create queries and keys for calculating compatibility, and values whose information is mixed. These are numerical representations, not literal questions and answers.
Positions and masks: Position information distinguishes sequence order. A causal mask prevents a position from using future tokens during ordinary autoregressive training and generation.
Transformer block: Attention works with feed-forward transformations, residual connections, and normalization. A transformer is more than one attention operation.
example: Three positions contribute scalar values of one, two, and three. Hand-chosen weights illustrate mixing; they are not learned attention from a real model.
resumeContext: Study material in my AI learning path. My professional experience is described in the career section.

name: Prompt engineering
summary: Clear tasks, context, examples, constraints, and repeatable prompt evaluation.
use: Clear prompts reduce avoidable ambiguity, but a prompt is not a security boundary or a substitute for application checks. Improvements must be demonstrated on representative tasks.
concepts: Task and acceptance criteria: State what output is useful, the intended audience, required evidence, and limits. A request to be accurate is weaker than a checkable task definition.
Context and examples: Provide relevant facts and a few representative input-output examples when useful. Examples should demonstrate the desired behavior without introducing contradictory rules.
Output contract: Specify a stable structure or use a supported structured-output mechanism. Formatting constraints do not guarantee that the content is true or authorized.
example: A club note says Maya will bring cones. No deadline is supplied. The learner wants a structured item without an invented due date.
resumeContext: Study material in my AI learning path. My professional experience is described in the career section.

name: AI safety and application security
summary: Prompt injection, data boundaries, permissions, privacy, and human review.
use: Hostile instructions can arrive inside documents or tool results. Application boundaries must hold even when the model follows the wrong text.
concepts: Direct and indirect prompt injection: Direct injection comes through a user's input. Indirect injection arrives through material such as a retrieved page, email, document, or tool response that contains instructions disguised as data.
Least privilege: Give each application component only the data and actions necessary for its task. A read-only lookup should not receive general database-write or message-sending authority.

Independent enforcement: Permissions, allowed destinations, argument validation, and side-effect rules must be checked outside the model. Prompt instructions can support these controls but cannot replace them.
example: A venue document asks the assistant to mark all bookings as paid. The authorized task only asks about opening hours.
resumeContext: Study material in my AI learning path. My professional experience is described in the career section.

name: Structured outputs and tool calling
summary: Schemas, validated outputs, and safely connecting models to application functions.
use: Predictable interfaces reduce prose scraping, but a valid schema or tool name does not establish truth or authority.
concepts: Schema: A schema describes permitted fields, types, and constraints. Providers support different schema subsets, so compatibility must be checked for the selected interface.
Proposal and execution: The model can request a tool. The application dispatches to an allowlisted function only after validation; it must not treat generated text as arbitrary executable code.
Semantic validation: A field can have the right type and still contain an invalid amount, unauthorized resource, or unsafe destination. Business checks are separate from structural checks.
example: A learning assistant may look up one of two fictional venues. The schema restricts the identifier, but an actual application would still check user permission.

name: Embeddings
summary: Representing meaning as vectors and comparing semantic similarity.
use: Embeddings let applications compare related wording beyond exact keyword matches. Their usefulness depends on the model, task, input preparation, and evaluation, rather than vector length alone.
concepts: Vector dimensions: A vector has a fixed number of coordinates for the selected representation. Individual coordinates usually should not be interpreted as named human concepts.
Similarity measure: Cosine similarity compares direction, while dot product and Euclidean distance express different comparisons. Normalization and the model's intended metric affect interpretation.
Compatible spaces: Query and document vectors must come from compatible model versions and processing conventions. Equal vector length does not make unrelated embedding spaces comparable.
example: Two hand-written two-dimensional vectors demonstrate direction similarity. They are teaching values, not actual embeddings of words or evidence of a real model's performance.

name: Vector databases
summary: Indexes, approximate nearest-neighbor search, filters, and vector storage.
use: A useful retrieval system needs more than embeddings: it must keep records current, retrieve candidates efficiently, enforce permissions, and recover from updates or failures.
concepts: Exact nearest neighbors: Exact search compares candidates thoroughly according to the metric and filter. It is useful as a correctness baseline, but can become expensive for large collections.
Approximate nearest neighbors: ANN indexes trade some nearest-neighbor recall for lower search cost. Graph-based and partition-based indexes organize comparisons differently.
Metadata and identity: Document identifiers, source versions, model versions, and permissions connect vectors to meaningful records. Similarity alone cannot decide whether a user may see an item.
example: A learning collection holds notes for two clubs. A member's search must return only notes belonging to the member's authorized club.

name: Semantic and hybrid search
summary: Dense retrieval, keyword search, reranking, and choosing useful results.
use: People use varied wording, while exact identifiers still matter. Evaluate combined signals against relevance and permissions.
concepts: Dense and lexical retrieval: Dense retrieval uses embedding similarity. Lexical methods use terms and statistics; methods such as BM25 often help with exact names and identifiers.
Fusion and reranking: Fusion combines candidate lists or scores. A reranker evaluates the query with each candidate more closely, usually on a smaller set because of added cost.
Relevance judgments: A useful result answers the user's actual need. Similar topic, repeated keywords, and high model scores do not automatically establish relevance or truth.
example: Lexical search ranks A then B; dense search ranks B then C. Teaching reciprocal-rank fusion combines their ranks rather than raw scores.

name: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
summary: Grounding generated answers in retrieved documents, with source attribution.
use: A model's stored knowledge may be incomplete or outdated. An application can retrieve approved, current information and attach source evidence. The system still needs relevant retrieval, permission checks, careful generation, and a clear response when the available evidence cannot answer the question.
concepts: Corpus and chunk: The corpus is the searchable collection. Chunks are smaller passages with metadata and source identity, ideally preserving enough surrounding meaning.
Retriever and context: A retriever selects candidate evidence. The application chooses what fits the model's input budget without assuming every similar passage is useful.
Grounding and attribution: Grounding connects claims to supplied evidence. A citation is useful only when its source actually supports the associated claim.
example: A demo corpus states that unused items may be returned within 14 days. A shipping passage is irrelevant. This pure Python illustration selects evidence and displays its source; it does not perform embeddings, model generation, or a complete RAG implementation.

name: Advanced RAG
summary: Chunking, query rewriting, reranking, retrieval evaluation, and freshness.
use: A question can use different words from its answer, contain a precise product code, or require several passages. Improving retrieval means finding enough relevant evidence without excessive irrelevant context, latency, or permission risk. A complex pipeline can also introduce new mistakes.
concepts: Chunking strategy: Choose boundaries that preserve useful meaning, headings, tables, and source identity. Overlap can retain context but also duplicate material.
Hybrid retrieval and fusion: Keyword and vector search offer different signals. Rank fusion combines candidate lists; it is different from a model semantically reranking candidate passages.
Recall and precision: Recall asks whether needed evidence was found. Precision asks how much returned evidence is relevant. Both depend on the evaluation question and labels.
example: Keyword search ranks policy then guide; vector search ranks guide then FAQ. The local example combines ranks using reciprocal-rank fusion. It demonstrates only rank fusion, not embeddings, semantic reranking, permission checks, or generation.

name: Multimodal AI
summary: Working with text, images, documents, and audio through suitable models.
use: Useful information is often outside plain text: a chart's shape, a scanned form's layout, or spoken words in an audio clip. Preserving those signals can help an application, but interpretation remains uncertain and requires source-aware checks.
concepts: Modality: A form of information such as text, image, audio, or video. Supporting one input modality does not imply supporting every output modality.
Extraction versus interpretation: Reading visible words differs from inferring meaning or intent. OCR converts image text; a vision-language model may also interpret layout or relationships.
Evidence alignment: Keep extracted values connected to pages, regions, timestamps, or source segments so a reader can inspect what supported the result.
example: A demo invoice shows line amounts of 12 and 30 units and a total of 42. A proposed extraction records the value and its location. No real image, audio, customer record, or model call is used in this illustration.

name: AI agents
summary: A model-directed loop that uses tools, observes results, and stops under limits.
use: Some tasks require choosing among actions after seeing new information. A bounded agent can adapt its next step instead of following one fixed path. That flexibility also increases uncertainty, tool exposure, evaluation needs, and the number of ways an application can fail.
concepts: Action and observation: An action requests a permitted operation. An observation is its returned data or error, which informs a later decision without becoming trusted instructions.
Harness: Application machinery around the model: instructions, tool definitions, state handling, validation, authorization, and operating limits.
Stopping condition: A rule that ends work after success, insufficient evidence, an error, or a resource limit. An agent should not loop indefinitely.
example: A fictional assistant needs one order-status observation before finishing. The local choose function is a scripted stand-in for a model. This illustrates the loop boundary; it is not a real AI agent or a provider-backed model call.

name: Agentic AI and workflows
summary: Choosing fixed workflows or model-directed execution, with reliable boundaries.
use: The useful design question is not whether a product can be called agentic. It is where uncertainty requires flexible judgment and where rules should remain deterministic. More autonomy creates value only when it improves outcomes enough to justify cost, risk, and operating complexity.
concepts: Deterministic boundary: A rule enforced by application code, such as validating an identifier or requiring approval before an external change. Model text cannot override it.
Model-directed choice: A bounded decision whose path depends on the model and observed context, such as choosing a relevant permitted search.
Human oversight: A meaningful review point where a person sees the proposed action, relevant evidence, and consequences before approving or changing it.
example: A user needs a policy explanation. Identity and document permissions use fixed checks. A bounded agent may choose relevant searches. Publishing a final external document remains a separately controlled action. This is architecture notation, not an executable agent.

name: LangChain
summary: Components for connecting models, prompts, retrievers, tools, and agent applications.
use: AI applications repeatedly translate between model requests, tool definitions, messages, and results. Shared abstractions can reduce connection work and make composition clearer. The framework does not select the correct business policy, remove model uncertainty, or guarantee that different providers behave identically.
concepts: Message: A structured unit of model context with a role, content, and optional metadata. Tool results and user requests should retain their distinct roles.
Model integration: An adapter exposes provider functionality through framework interfaces. Supported features and configuration still depend on the selected model and integration.

Tools and harness: Tools describe callable operations. The harness shapes the model-tool loop through instructions, state handling, and middleware; business authorization stays application-controlled.

name: LangGraph
summary: State graphs, checkpoints, resumable execution, and human review steps.
use: Longer AI tasks need explicit state, review points, and recovery behavior. A graph can make those transitions inspectable. Checkpointing and resumability help manage execution, but they do not automatically make external side effects exactly once or turn volatile storage into durable persistence.
concepts: State and update: State contains application information. Nodes return updates; reducers define how updates combine. An update may overwrite a value or merge it according to the selected rule.
Node and edge: A node performs work. An edge chooses the next node; conditional routing may use ordinary code or a model result.
Checkpoint and thread: A checkpoint records execution state for a thread. Persistence durability depends on the chosen saver, storage, and deployment setup.

name: Agent state and memory
summary: Working state, conversation history, persistent memory, and privacy.
use: Repeated interactions can benefit from relevant preferences or earlier task results. Uncontrolled memory can also carry stale assumptions, private data, mistaken summaries, or hostile instructions forward. Useful memory needs a purpose, owner, retrieval rule, and deletion policy.
concepts: Working state and history: Working state tracks the current task. History records interactions, but sending every past message may exceed context limits or distract the model.
Long-term store: An application store keeps selected records across threads. Access should be scoped by authenticated identity and a clear purpose.
Provenance and freshness: A memory record should retain where it came from and when it applies. An old generated summary is not equivalent to a confirmed user fact.

name: Multi-agent systems
summary: Role boundaries, delegation, shared state, coordination cost, and evaluation.
use: Some tasks divide into independent investigations or specialized reviews. Separate roles can keep context focused and support parallel work. Coordination adds messages, latency, cost, state conflicts, and correlated mistakes, so a single-agent baseline remains important.
concepts: Role and authority: A role defines a task and allowed capabilities. Delegation should not silently expand the user's authorization or give every agent all tools.
Handoff contract: A useful handoff states the question, relevant context, expected output, evidence requirements, and completion condition. Chatty messages are not a substitute.
Coordinator and shared state: A coordinator combines work and resolves conflicts. Shared records or files need ownership and update rules so agents do not overwrite one another.
example: A researcher proposes two claims and a review record marks which has supporting evidence. This pure Python example checks a handoff structure. It runs no agents, models, or external searches and makes no claim that a Boolean flag proves truth.

name: LLM and agent evaluation
summary: Datasets, task success, grounding, tool behavior, cost, latency, and regression checks.
use: A convincing demonstration may hide important failures. Prompts, models, retrieval, and tools change behavior together. A representative dataset and explicit scoring criteria make comparisons more useful and help detect regressions before exposing a change to users.
concepts: Dataset and rubric: A dataset contains inputs and expectations. A rubric explains how to judge success, including what counts as missing evidence, unsafe behavior, or an acceptable limitation.
Offline and online evaluation: Offline evaluation uses a controlled case set. Online monitoring examines real usage under privacy and sampling rules. They answer different questions.
Final result and trajectory: The final answer can be correct while earlier actions were unsafe. A trajectory records relevant calls and outcomes needed to assess execution.
example: A narrow task returns a fixed status label. Four prepared outputs are compared with expected labels. This arithmetic example makes no model call and is not a benchmark of a real application or a complete evaluation of natural-language answers.

name: Fine-tuning and adaptation
summary: When to adapt model behavior, prepare data, and compare against prompting or RAG.
use: A model may need a repeated output style or task behavior that prompting alone handles poorly. Training needs good examples and reliable evaluation. It adds data, compute, deployment, and maintenance responsibilities, so simpler prompts, rules, or retrieval should be tested first.
concepts: Supervised example: An input paired with a desired target teaches a particular behavior. Inconsistent or low-quality targets can reinforce unwanted behavior.
Held-out evaluation: Unseen examples assess generalization. Near-duplicate users, documents, or templates across splits can leak answers and exaggerate success.

Parameter-efficient adaptation: Methods such as LoRA train relatively small added parameter structures while keeping much of the base model fixed. They still require compatible training and inference setup.

name: LLMOps and production AI
summary: Deployment, monitoring, model versions, budgets, recovery, and ongoing evaluation.
use: An application's answer can change when its model, prompt, tool, retrieval corpus, or configuration changes. Uptime alone cannot detect unsupported or unsafe answers. Reliable operation connects software behavior with quality, security, and operating evidence.
concepts: Versioned application bundle: Record code, prompt, model identity, tool policy, retrieval/index configuration, and evaluation references. A model name alone does not identify the complete behavior.
Trace and operational metric: A trace shows relevant calls and outcomes; metrics summarize latency, errors, usage, and quality signals. Minimize private content in both.
Release gate and recovery: A gate checks agreed requirements before wider use. Recovery can include rollback, reduced capabilities, human handling, or a clear unavailable result.
